::: {.lp-lede}
Instructing Machines is a fourteen-week introduction to programming for
molecular biology, written for students who will have a model at their side
from the first line they type. Every week pairs a piece of Python with a way
of working alongside an AI and a way of checking what it hands back.
:::

::: {.lp-actions}
[Start here <i class="bi bi-arrow-right"></i>](python/getting_started.ipynb){.lp-btn}
:::

<!-- [14 weeks &middot; 65 chapters &middot; 8 projects on real data &middot; 7 interactive
widgets &middot; MIT licensed]{.lp-counts} -->

:::


::: {.grid .lp-audiences}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}

[<i class="bi bi-mortarboard-fill"></i> For students]{.lp-audience-label}

### 15 minutes to get started {.unnumbered}

The course folder, Python, the editor and the terminal are all set up in one
pass, most of which is waiting. By the end of the course you can:

::: {.lp-list}
- Read code the way the machine does.
- Write Python to solve small problems.
- Break a problem into sub-problems and write them as testable functions.
- Verify code written by an AI, or by someone else.
- Judge how much of a task to hand over, and how much to keep.
- Explain why an AI is only as useful to you as your ability to check it.
:::

<!-- [Getting started <i class="bi bi-arrow-right"></i>](python/getting_started.ipynb){.lp-btn} -->

### Take it and make it yours {.unnumbered}

Built for undergraduates in Molecular Biology and Molecular Medicine at
[Aarhus University](https://kursuskatalog.au.dk/en/course/133215/Bioinformatics),
and [MIT licensed](https://opensource.org/license/mit). If you teach a similar
course, fork it.

::: {.lp-list}
- Notes, slides, exercises and projects, all in the repository
- Seven notebook widgets, installable as packages
- A JupyterLite demo, so students can try before installing
- A written account of the course design and the AI arc
- [A live demo of the same material runs in the browser through
[JupyterLite](demo/lab/index.html).]
- Fork it on github <i class="bi bi-github"></i>
:::

### Teaching AI in programming {.unnumbered}

The [course design](planning/course-design.qmd) describes the reasoning behind how AI is taught and integrated in different ways across the course but, in a nutshell, it is this simple:

::: {.lp-thesis}
An AI is useful to you up to the limit of what you can specify and verify. The course spends fourteen weeks raising that limit.
:::

::: {.lp-panels}

::: {.lp-panel}
[<i class="bi bi-person"></i> Brain]{.lp-panel-label}

Your training is what lets you ask a questions about molecular biology and judge answers you are handed.
:::

::: {.lp-panel}
[<i class="bi bi-code-slash"></i> Code]{.lp-panel-label}

Python lets you write machine instructions in something close to the plain English you think in.
:::

::: {.lp-panel}
[<i class="bi bi-stars"></i> AI]{.lp-panel-label}

An AI can turn a problem posed in English into Python code that you can test and verify.
:::

::: {.lp-panel}
[<i class="bi bi-cpu"></i> CPU]{.lp-panel-label}

Once your question is expressed in as Python code, running it on you computer produces the answer.
:::

:::

Say computing the GC content of a DNA sequence was a very complex problem. You can only ask an AI to produce the code for you if you can **specify** that it is "the fraction of bases in a DNA sequence that are G or C":

```python
def gc_content(seq):
    gc = seq.count("G") + seq.count("C")
    return gc / len(seq)
```

and you can only **verify** that you got what you asked for if you can define tests that only correct code will pass:

```python
assert gc_content("GCGC") == 1.0
assert gc_content("ATAT") == 0.0
```

### What the material looks like {.unnumbered}

The notes are executable notebooks. Exercises come with widgets that step
through code line by line, so a claim about what the machine does can be
settled on the spot.
